newsitem.title: USA: U.S. lawmakers back Albright on HK boycott.
newsitem.headline: U.S. lawmakers back Albright on HK boycott.

text.p: Members of Congress said on Tuesday they would join Secretary of State Madeleine Albright in boycotting the swearing-in of a new China-backed legislature in Hong Kong.

"Our delegation, which is committed to reaffirm support for Hong Kong's democratic system, will not attend any swearing-in ceremony for the provisional legislature," Representative Christopher Cox, a California Republican who heads the House of Representative side of the delegation said in a letter to Albright.

Cox commended Albright's decision, announced on Monday, not to attend the legislature swearing-in when she visits Hong Kong on June 30-July 1 for ceremonies concerning the handover of the British colony to China at midnight.

"This body was chosen not by the 6 million people of Hong Kong but by a selection committee of 400 which was itself hand-picked by a 150-member preparatory committee" chaired by Chinese Foreign Minister Qian Qichen, he said.

"Particularly because the swearing-in of Beijing's appointees also accomplishes the swearing-out of the democratically elected representatives of the people of Hong Kong, both principle and prudence indicate that representatives of the United States should not dignify such a proceeding," Cox said.

Sen. Frank Murkowski, an Alaskan Republican heading the Senate delegation to the Hong Kong revision to China, told Albright at a Senate Finance Committee hearing: "I assume that we are likely to follow your lead."

Albright, expanding on comments Monday by her spokesman, told the panel: "I have decided that if invited to go to ... a hypothetical installation of the non-elected legislative council, that I personally would not attend that, and that it is important for us to make clear that we, at a high level, do not endorse what they are doing."

She made her comments during a hearing in which she vigorously argued for renewal of Most Favoured Nation trade benefits for China, which some lawmakers want to scrap because of U.S. concerns over Hong Kong, human rights, arms sales, a trade deficit and other issues.

Nevertheless, China fired back a propaganda volley against her decision to boycott the legislature swearing-in, accusing certain people in the United States of harbouring "evil intentions" towards Hong Kong ahead of its return to Chinese rule.

China had planned to swear in future leader Tung Chee-hwa, the future judiciary and the provisional chamber on July 1, shortly after a solemn midnight flag ceremony marking the end of 156 years of British rule and reunion with China.
"We have never believed that the appointment of a provisional legislature is justified or necessary," State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said on Monday.
"There is a pefectly good legislature in place, it's a democratically elected legislature for the people of Hong Kong, the Legislative Council," he added.
